# Dagda: canonical, contested, and the false forms on record

The internet spells **Dagda** more ways than one, and only one of them is the name the sources wrote. This is the register's ruling — canonical, fallback, contested, and false, each in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Dagda
- **Original script:** —
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Convention:** the tradition’s own scholarly transliteration standard
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 93 of 437

## The Canonical Form

The tradition's record preserves this name in its romanized scholarly form: **Dagda** — no older script survives to transcribe, so the canonical content is the exactness of the spelling itself.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form the tradition’s convention demands.

## Where the Flattened Form Stands

The plain form *dagda* differs from the canonical **Dagda** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## The Register of False Forms

No circulating form of this name currently qualifies as false under the register's standard — a rare standing. The spelling is short, sturdy, and rarely mangled.

## The Contested Forms

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — the tradition’s standard — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Dagda**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## What the Address Bar Allows

IDNA 2008 permits the letters these restorations use — macrons, acutes, underdots, thorn, ogonek, the lot — and the DNS carries them as punycode (`xn--` labels). Two honest constraints remain. First, **registrar inventory**: the protocol permits a character; the registrar's stock decides whether the exact domain can be bought today. Second, **combined marks**: forms like *Apṓllōn* (acute stacked on a macron) are philologically ideal yet effectively untypeable on phones and unsupported across much of the registration system.

That is why the rulebook keeps a fallback hierarchy — full restoration first, then the circumflex when the source carries one, then the macron-only academic standard, then an attested variant, and only as a last resort the plain ASCII form. **Every step down the ladder is still defensible; nothing on the ladder is a wrong mark.** A fallback is a choice among attested forms. A false form is not on the ladder at all.

## Where the Name Stood First

The Dagda is a textual god: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. His manuscript witnesses are exact — Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, which is the basis of Gray's edition, while Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the Book of Leinster and its sister codices. His mythic address, by contrast, is one of the most famous pieces of architecture in Europe: Brú na Bóinne, the Bend of the Boyne, where the passage tomb of Newgrange (c. 3200 BCE) has stood for five thousand years on the site the tales call the Dagda's Brug and Óengus's síd. The nearest material kin of his iconography is Gaulish: the altar from Sarrebourg showing Sucellos with his mallet and pot beside Nantosuelta is the standard comparison for the good god with the club and the vessel — comparative evidence, never identification. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Verdict

The register rules for **Dagda**, and the ruling is checkable: every mark sourced, every violation stated, every borderline form given its honest standing. *dagda* carries the name freely — it differs only in display, and the register says so without reservation. Anything else in circulation has its origin and its failure recorded above. That is the whole of the law on this name — and the temple at [/dagda/](/dagda/) enforces it.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 9 cited sources — Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired), ed. and trans. Elizabeth A. Gray — Bres' forts, the porridge pit, the ford of the Unius, the harp on the wall, Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. R. A. S. Macalister — the eighty-year kingship; his death at the Brug from Cethlenn's wound, Tochmarc Étaíne (The Wooing of Étaín), ed. Bergin and Best — the birth of Óengus; the day the sun stood still.
